title: Should you size a market from the buyers' side or the sellers' side?
description: Market sizing for case interviews. "How big is the market for X?" Say your approach before any maths. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: Every market sizing question can be built from one of two directions: start from the buyers, or start from the sellers. Knowing both gives you a choice, and a way to check your answer. Here they are side by side.
body:
When it helps

"How big is the market for X?" Say your approach before any maths.

The checklist

Demand side (start from buyers)

  • Population
  • × share in target segment
  • × share who buy
  • × units a year
  • × price

Supply side (start from sellers)

  • Number of sellers or sites
  • × sales or capacity each
  • × price

Sanity check

  • Compare with a number you know
  • Does the per-person figure feel right?

An example

Say you are asked how many electric scooters are sold in Spain each year. From the buyers' side: people in Spain, times the share who live in cities, times the share who would own a scooter, divided by how many years a scooter lasts. From the sellers' side: the number of shops and online stores selling scooters, times how many each sells a year. If the two answers land in the same range, you can be confident.

How it sounds in an interview

I could size this from the buyers' side or the sellers' side. I'll start with buyers, because I can estimate those more easily, then cross-check with the number of shops if we have time.

Decide what counts before estimating

Suppose the interviewer asks for the annual market for home coffee machines. Does "market" mean machines sold this year, machines already installed, or the value of machines and capsules together? Those are three different answers. Confirm the unit, geography, buyer and period before choosing a calculation.

A demand-side estimate could start with 30 million households, assume 40% own a machine and replace it every six years: 30m × 40% ÷ 6 = 2 million replacement machines annually. Add first-time buyers separately. A supply-side check might use units sold by retailers, multiplied by the number of major outlets and their sales volume. These are made-up practice assumptions, not UK market statistics.

The useful question is not which method is "correct", but which assumptions you can explain. If one assumed replacement life changes from six to eight years, replacement demand falls from 2 million to 1.5 million, a 25% reduction. Tell the interviewer that this assumption drives your estimate and suggest how you would test it.
